items.title: Button forms read their fields in one shared way
items.where_users_meet_it: The one-button forms: Make active and Remove on Settings → Characters, plus the admin buttons (Unlink, Reassign, Force logout, the role toggle, Retry on a dead-lettered ESI job, and the statics Check feed now, Promote and Reject).
items.before: Each of these eight routes picked its fields out of the form in its own way and wrote its own error wording. A request whose body wasn't a readable form crashed the route, and the answer was a server error. Only a hand-made or broken request does that; the buttons always send a proper form.
items.after: Nothing changes for anyone using the buttons. A request that isn't a readable form now gets a plain 'bad request' refusal instead of a server error. A bad field is reported as 'Invalid' plus the field's name.
items.behind_the_scenes: There is now one shared form reader. Each route lists the fields it expects. The reader picks out only those fields, checks them, and writes the refusal itself. The eight hand-written pickers, each with its own error wording, are gone. The reader also catches a body it can't read, so a garbled request no longer crashes the route.
items.risk_notes: Low. A missing field is still rejected exactly as before. The wording inside the raw refusal changes (for example 'Invalid characterId'), but no page, client or test depends on it. A garbled post is now counted on the health dashboard as a rejected request, not an unexpected error. Rejected requests stay out of the success rate.

items.title: Admin forms, Delete account and Feedback move onto the shared save pipeline
items.where_users_meet_it: The admin role toggle, statics review buttons, Reassign and ESI job Retry; the Delete account dialog; the Feedback dialog.
items.before: These six routes wired up their own checks by hand, and the four admin forms went through a separate admin-only gate. Feedback read the message and counted it against the five-a-minute allowance before it checked that the post came from our own site.
items.after: Real users see the same results: the same redirects, the same messages, and the same order of checks for the admin routes and Delete account. Feedback now refuses a post from another website first, before reading it and before it counts against the allowance. A junk post from another site now gets 'not allowed' instead of 'bad request'. Feedback from the site itself, signed in or not, works as before.
items.behind_the_scenes: Most save routes already went through one shared pipeline. Its steps are: an optional rate limit, the sign-in or admin check, the same-site check, reading the body, then the work. These six routes now use it too. The separate admin gate did the same thing, so it is deleted. Feedback is public, so it gets an 'anyone may post' pass, but it still goes through the same-site check, which now runs before the body is read.
items.risk_notes: Low. Reviewers checked each route's order of checks. The admin routes still run the admin check, then the same-site check, then the form, as before. Delete account still applies its rate limit first. The admin routes had no rate limit before and still have none. Nothing still refers to the deleted gate. The capability names the dashboard groups by are unchanged.

items.title: Failed button actions now count as failures on the health dashboard
items.where_users_meet_it: The admin health dashboard: the 'Mutations' success line and the failed-operations breakdown under it.
items.before: Some button actions fail and send you back with a notice: Remove character can't finish, an admin unlink can't complete, or Check feed now finds a refresh already running or the community feed down. The dashboard logged each of these as a success, so it overstated how well actions were going.
items.after:
Each failure is now logged with its real kind:
- Remove character failing is an unexpected error.
- An admin unlink that can't complete, or a 'refresh already running', is a conflict.
- 'Feed unavailable' is a service being down.

The 'not your character' and 'only character' refusals count as rejected requests. Those stay out of the success rate and only add to the rejected count. People see the same pages and notices. Only the dashboard numbers change, and the Mutations rate may read a little lower.
items.behind_the_scenes: One helper now builds the 'go back to this page' redirect that every button form answers with. When the redirect reports a problem, the helper also tells telemetry what kind of problem it was. Four home-made copies of the redirect and four inline ones are gone. The redirect addresses are unchanged.
items.risk_notes: Users see no change. The Mutations line turns amber below 99% and red below 95%. On a quiet day, a few 'refresh already running' or 'feed unavailable' presses could be enough to turn it amber. Successful redirects record nothing extra. Not screenshot-able: both test servers share one database, so their dashboards would show the same totals.
items.owner_question: Should pressing Check feed now while another statics refresh is already running count as a failed action on the health dashboard? It now counts as a conflict, which can tip the Mutations line amber on a quiet day. It could instead be treated like a rejected request and left out of the rate.

items.title: Early refusals are checked against each route's written list of answers
items.where_users_meet_it: Nowhere visible. It covers the JSON save routes behind settings, the planner, structures, maps, preferences, feedback and location sharing.
items.before: Sometimes the shared pipeline refuses a request early: not signed in, from another site, or a body it can't read. It sent those answers without checking them against the route's written list of the answers it may give.
items.after: The same answers go out, because every route's list already includes them. If a later change adds an early refusal that a route doesn't list, tests now fail loudly instead of the route quietly answering something undocumented.
items.behind_the_scenes: A route can now hand its written contract to the shared pipeline. The pipeline then sends its early refusals through the same checked path the route's own answers use. Two routes that worked out their error status by hand now go through the contract as well: the internal token route and the location-sharing 'leave' call.
items.risk_notes: Low. The new check throws if a contract doesn't list a refusal. Reviewers compared each contracted route's refusals with its contract, and all match. The admin and form routes pass no contract, so nothing changes for them.

items.title: An edited notice code in the address bar no longer crashes the page
items.where_users_meet_it: Settings → Characters, an admin user's page, and admin Wormhole statics. It only happens when someone opens a hand-edited link.
items.before: These pages pick a notice from a code in the address (?error= or ?outcome=). Some codes, such as 'constructor' or 'toString', broke the page: instead of the page, you got the 'Pod malfunction / This page couldn't load' error panel.
items.after: Unknown codes are now just unknown. The Characters page shows its usual general notice, 'Linking was cancelled or failed.' The admin user page shows 'That action could not be completed.' The statics page shows no banner. Real codes show the same messages as before.
items.behind_the_scenes: One small function now turns an address-bar code into notice text, and it accepts only codes that are really on that page's list. Before, each page looked the code up in a plain table. Every table quietly carries a few built-in names such as 'constructor', which matched a hidden function instead of text, and the page fell over trying to show it. Each page's list is now also tied to the exact codes its buttons send, so a missing message is caught when the code is built.
items.risk_notes: Very low. A missing code or a repeated one still shows nothing, as before. The new home-page notice for a refused sign-in (?error=account_not_linked) from the account-takeover fix uses this same function; it is described with that fix.

items.title: Three refusals now return to the page with a notice instead of raw error text
items.where_users_meet_it: Make active on Settings → Characters; Unlink on an admin user's page; Promote and Reject on admin Wormhole statics.
items.before:
In three cases the browser left the site and showed a bare block of JSON error text:
- Pressing Make active for a character that is no longer on your account, for example from an old tab after removing it.
- An admin pressing Unlink for a character that has already left that user.
- Pressing Promote or Reject on a statics snapshot that is no longer pending (double-clicking Promote is the easiest way), or pressing Promote on one with nothing in it.
items.after:
Each now returns to the page you were on with a notice:
- On Characters: 'That character isn't linked to your account.'
- On the admin user page: 'That character isn't linked to this user.' This message is new.
- On statics: 'That snapshot is no longer pending review, so nothing changed.' or 'That snapshot has no static assignments, so it was not promoted.' Both messages are new.

Nothing else on these pages changes.
items.behind_the_scenes: These three refusals now use the same 'back to the page with a notice' redirect as the other refusals on these forms. The admin user page and the statics page got the new messages to show.
items.risk_notes:
Low. Telemetry records the same failure kinds as the old error answers. The redirects go to fixed pages. The admin one includes the user's id, which is checked to be plain letters, digits, dashes and underscores, so it can't send anyone off-site.

One wording quirk: after a double-click on Promote, the second click's answer is what you see. So the admin reads 'That snapshot is no longer pending review, so nothing changed' even though the first click did promote it. The Serving copy card on the same page shows the new version.
items.owner_question:
Four admin buttons still answer a refusal with raw JSON error text instead of a notice:
- Reassign, when the character is already yours or has left that user.
- The role toggle, on your own role or for a user who is gone.
- Force logout, on yourself or for a user who is gone.
- Retry on an ESI job that is no longer dead-lettered, for example after a double-click.

Should those be converted in a later wave? Also, is the 'nothing changed' wording after a double-clicked Promote acceptable, or should it say the snapshot was already handled?

items.title: Background character checks run on more requests; map-access deliveries are shared across visits
items.where_users_meet_it: Nowhere on screen. It runs in the background while a signed-in player uses the site.
items.before: While a player is on the site, it re-checks each of their characters' EVE access in the background, at most once a day per character, and delivers any queued updates to who can see which shared maps. Page views started this, but many actions did not: switching the active character, removing a character, deleting the account, revoking sessions, the corporation sharing toggle, the admin actions, the Atlas page and the Industry structures panel. Each visit also started its own delivery of queued map-access updates, so at busy moments many identical deliveries ran at once.
items.after: Those actions and pages now start the same background check. It runs after the response is sent, so nothing gets slower. On each server, visits now share one delivery of queued map-access updates every 15 seconds, and a failed delivery is tried again on the next visit. Updates the site has just queued itself are still delivered straight away. Nothing changes on screen. At most, a map-access update that waits for a visit to deliver it can arrive up to 15 seconds later.
items.behind_the_scenes: There were two ways to read who is logged in, and only one of them started the background check. Every guard now uses that one shared session read. The delivery of queued map-access updates started by visits goes through a small gate that lets one run through every 15 seconds per server. The Industry structures panel and the corporation-sharing action also stop reading the session twice.
items.risk_notes: Low risk. EVE traffic doesn't grow, because each character is still checked at most once a day. No scheduled job empties the map-access queue, so it still depends on visits. That is why the window is kept short. The optional lease that would stop two servers delivering the same update was skipped, because it needs a database migration. Duplicate deliveries are harmless.

items.title: One shared definition of 'this character belongs to this account'
items.where_users_meet_it: Nowhere a player would notice. The only visible effect is on the 'Add character' button when the connection drops.
items.before: About five places had their own hand-written copy of the rule for 'this character belongs to this account'. If the request behind 'Add character' failed, for example because the connection dropped, the browser logged an uncaught error. On a development server Next.js showed its red error overlay. For players the button simply did nothing.
items.after: Every place uses one shared rule, which finds exactly the same characters as before. A failed 'Add character' request is now caught quietly. The button still does nothing, as players already saw, but there is no uncaught error.
items.behind_the_scenes: The ownership rule and the join that links an account to its character profile now come from one shared module. The internal name for EVE as a login provider now comes from one place, instead of three, one of which pulled in server-only code. The admin search by character name now joins on the character number rather than comparing text, with the same results. 'Add character' handles a failed start the same way 'Log in' already did.
items.risk_notes: Low risk. Reviewers checked that every rewritten rule finds the same rows as before. Nothing changes for players.

items.title: The EVE login app's credentials are read in one place
items.where_users_meet_it: Nowhere on screen.
items.before: The site's EVE app ID and secret were looked up separately by the three pieces that talk to EVE's login service: finishing a login, refreshing a character's access, and revoking it when a character or account is removed. Each one passed them along.
items.after: The one piece that builds the request to EVE reads them itself. Logging in, refreshing and revoking work exactly as before.
items.behind_the_scenes: The ID and secret are read when each request is built, not passed in by every caller. The failure cases are kept: a missing credential still fails loudly at login and on refresh, and is not mistaken for an EVE outage on that character's record. A revoke during account or character removal still never blocks the removal.
items.risk_notes: Low risk. It only matters if the server is missing its EVE credentials, and that case behaves as before.

items.title: Removed helpers that only passed calls along (including the live-map login token)
items.where_users_meet_it: Nowhere visibly. The affected areas are the Delete account dialog, live maps (the Convex connection) and character access refreshes.
items.before: Several small helpers did nothing but forward to another function. One handed the live-map service its login token. One checked whether the 'I understand' box in Delete account was ticked. Two forms had identical copies of the same input rule. One read the EVE request budget, and one re-checked a stored EVE token.
items.after: Callers use the underlying functions directly. Live maps get their login token the same way. In Delete account, the Confirm button still stays disabled until the box is ticked. Switching or removing a character checks the posted character the same way, and a character's stored EVE access is judged the same way.
items.behind_the_scenes: These pass-through layers were deleted, and their callers now call the real function. The two identical character form rules became one. The stored-token check now reuses the normal cached-token check, after the same three early checks it had before.

The screenshot kit can't check the live-map login on its review servers (a known limit). Open a live map while signed in on staging after the promote to confirm it.

items.title: Logging in with a character removed from an account no longer opens that old account
items.where_users_meet_it: Logging in with EVE from the home page or any Log in button, with a character that used to be on an account, for example after a character sale, or after someone removed one of their own characters.
items.before: Behind the scenes, each account carries a hidden address named after the character it last logged in with. Removing that character, whether by the player in Settings, Characters or by an admin, didn't update the address. The next person to log in with that character, such as its buyer, was matched to the old account by that address. They were signed straight into it, with its other characters, maps and settings, and the character was quietly added back. A related bug: a character moved to a new owner's account through 'Add character' could fail to log in on its own, because the old account still held its address.
items.after: A login with a character that isn't on any account always gets its own new account holding just that character. The old account is untouched and keeps its other characters. A character that was moved with 'Add character' logs in to its new account normally. If the clean-up at login ever fails, the login is refused rather than risk the wrong account. The player lands on the home page with a short explanation (see the next item). One side effect: a player who removes one of their own characters and later logs in with it directly now gets a separate new account, rather than going back into their old one. Logging in with their main character and using 'Add character' merges it back, as the site already does for a player's own characters.
items.behind_the_scenes: There are three safeguards. First, the login library is told never to join a login to an account by that hidden address. A character joins an account only through 'Add character' while logged in. Second, the address is repaired at three points: when a character is removed, when that character next logs in (before the account lookup), and once for all existing accounts by a database update that runs with this deploy. That update first moves every outdated address to a per-account placeholder that no login can match. Then it gives each account the address of its oldest remaining character. No account is deleted. Third, the login library's own 'unlink' entry point is switched off, so every removal goes through the site's path, which repairs the address.
items.risk_notes: This can't be screenshotted, because it needs a real EVE login. Tests against a real database cover it with the real login library: unlink then log in as the owner or a buyer, an outdated address left by older code, a failed repair (refused, nothing changes), 'Add character' while an old address still names the character, and the raw unlink being refused. Migration 0083 rewrites only the hidden addresses, which are never shown anywhere. Each login now runs one extra small database lookup. This fix stops new cases only: any character already pulled into the wrong account before this ships stays there until an admin moves it.
items.owner_question: Two decisions. (1) Is it acceptable that a player who removes their own character and later logs in with it directly gets a separate new account? They can merge it back with 'Add character' from their main. (2) Do you want a one-off check of staging and production for accounts that may already have taken in a character this way, so an admin can move any back?

items.after: Failed logins go straight to the home page in every environment. items.title: Signing in with a character can no longer drop you into someone else's account
items.where_users_meet_it: The 'Log in with EVE Online' button (and the command palette and planner sign-in), Settings → Characters (Unlink and Add character), admins unlinking or reassigning characters, and the home page after a refused sign-in.
items.before: Every account carries a hidden sign-in address. It is named after the character the account last signed in with directly. When that character was unlinked in Settings → Characters, or by an admin, the address still pointed at it. The next time anyone signed in directly with that character, the sign-in system matched the address, quietly attached the character back onto the old account, and signed them in to it. Here are the four cases on staging today. One: you unlink your main, then sign in with it later. You land back in your old account and the main reappears in your list, so the unlink didn't stick. Two: you buy a character whose seller had unlinked it. If it was the character the seller last signed in with, you land in the seller's account, with their other characters, maps, plans and settings, and admin rights if they had them. Three: you buy a character the seller never unlinked. EVE reports a new owner, so the site moves the character out of the seller's account and gives you a fresh account. That case already worked. Four: you add a character while signed in, under Settings → Characters → Add character. It joins your account. But if an old account's hidden address still named that character, signing in directly with it later failed with a server error.
items.after: Characters now join an account only through Add character while you are signed in. A direct sign-in never attaches a character to an account by its hidden address. One: unlink your main, then sign in with it. You get a separate, brand-new account that holds just that character, and your old account keeps everything else. To bring the character back, sign in with a character still on the old account and use Add character. The site's existing account merge then folds the two accounts together. Two: buy a character someone unlinked. You get a brand-new account with only that character, and the seller's account is untouched. Three: buy a character that was sold without unlinking. Same as before: you get a fresh account and the seller loses that character. If it was the seller's only character, their empty account is removed, as it is today. Four: add a character while signed in. It works as before, and signing in directly with it afterwards also works, because sign-in now clears any stale address before it looks anything up. If that clean-up itself fails, for example during a database hiccup, the sign-in is refused rather than risk the wrong account. You land on the home page with a notice: 'That character isn't linked to an account here any more. Try signing in again, or sign in with a character on your account and add it under Settings → Characters.' Other failed sign-ins, such as cancelling on EVE's login page, still land on the home page with no message, as they already do in production.
items.behind_the_scenes: Three changes work together. First, the sign-in library's 'link by matching address' feature is switched off. A direct sign-in now either finds the character's own link or creates a new account. Second, whenever a character leaves an account, its hidden address is moved to the account's oldest remaining character while the account is locked. That covers a Settings unlink, an admin unlink, a reassign, and a sale detected at sign-in. If another account already holds that address, this account gets a private placeholder that no sign-in can ever match, instead of an error. Third, every direct sign-in first checks whether some other account's address still names the character, and repairs it before the lookup. So leftovers from older code, or from a failed clean-up, can't strand anyone or cause a collision. The sign-in buttons now ask for any failure to come back to the home page, and the home page explains the one refusal a user can act on.
items.risk_notes: A new end-to-end test drives the real sign-in and the real Settings unlink against Postgres, with only EVE's token exchange faked. It covers: an unlink followed by a sign-in from the owner and from a buyer; a stale address left by old code; a repair that cannot run (the sign-in is refused and nothing is linked); a sale without an unlink; Add character while a stale address exists; and freeing a stale holder. The real behaviour change is for people who used to unlink a character and sign back in with it: they now get a second account until they use Add character. This relies on Better Auth 1.6.30's disableImplicitLinking switch. The sign-in-time repair runs on every EVE sign-in: it is one extra indexed lookup, plus a locked write only when a stale holder exists. The notice copy says 'isn't linked to an account here any more', which is slightly off when the cause was a database error, but it still gives the right next step. In local dev on staging, a failed sign-in showed Better Auth's own error page. Production already redirected home, so the only production difference is the new notice. The unlink half of the fix is listed under P161, and the one-off repair of existing accounts under migration 0083.
items.owner_question: Signing in directly with a character you previously unlinked now always opens a separate new account, instead of putting you back in your old one. Is that what you want? If so, should Settings → Characters say it near the Unlink button (for example: 'Signing in with an unlinked character later starts a new account; use Add character to bring it back')?

items.title: One shared unlink path for Settings unlink, admin unlink and admin reassign
items.where_users_meet_it: Settings → Characters → Unlink, and on an admin's view of a user, Unlink and 'Reassign to me'.
items.before: The three ways a character leaves an account each did their own clean-up. Settings unlink and admin unlink revoked map access, removed the character, and moved the active character when needed. They never touched the account's hidden sign-in address, and that gap is what made the takeover possible. Reassign repaired the address in a separate second step. If that step failed, the failure was only written to the logs, and the admin was sent back to their own user page as if everything had worked.
items.after: All three now run the same steps in the same order and finish with the same account tidy-up. If you removed the active character, the active character moves to the oldest remaining one. The hidden address moves off the removed character. An account left with no characters is removed, which can only happen when two unlinks race, because removing your last character is still refused. In normal use nothing on screen changes: you land on the same page, the character is gone, and the notices are the same. There is one visible difference for admins. If the final tidy-up fails after a reassign has already moved the character, which takes a rare database error, the admin now sees a plain server error page instead of being returned to their user page. The character has still moved.
items.behind_the_scenes: One 'unlink a character' routine now owns the whole sequence. It revokes the character's map access, removes or moves the account link, restores access if the removal failed, finishes the map clean-up, and then settles the account. Each caller supplies only how to remove the link and how to report a failure. Settings uses the sign-in library's own unlink, admin unlink deletes the link, and reassign moves it to the admin. The reassign page has lost its own second, error-swallowing tidy-up. Admin unlink also reads the user's character list once instead of twice.
items.risk_notes: New Postgres tests fail on the old code: the address was left on the removed character on the admin and direct-removal paths, and on a reassign where the source keeps other characters. The first draft skipped the map and tracking refresh when the tidy-up failed; bbbec30d fixes that, and it is listed as its own item. Since the takeover fix, the address repair no longer errors when the new address is taken; it falls back to a placeholder. A database outage is now the realistic way to reach the reassign error page. The not_linked notice change on admin unlink belongs to P255, not this item.
items.owner_question: When the tidy-up after a reassign fails, the admin now sees a plain server error page, even though the character did move. Is that acceptable? Or would you rather they were redirected back to the admin page with a notice such as 'Moved, but the source account could not be tidied up; try again'?

items.title: A failed account tidy-up after an unlink still finishes the map and tracking refresh
items.where_users_meet_it: Only after an unlink or reassign whose final account tidy-up fails: Settings → Characters → Unlink, admin Unlink, and admin 'Reassign to me'.
items.before: On staging, after a character leaves an account, the site always refreshes the maps that involve that character, stops location tracking for it on the old account, and recalculates the account's roster value, even when a later step fails. The first wave 9 version of the shared unlink routine would have skipped those follow-ups if the account tidy-up failed.
items.after: The follow-ups always run once the character has actually been removed or moved, and only then is the error reported. On a reassign that includes refreshing the receiving admin's roster. Compared with staging there is no visible change. This keeps staging's behaviour. A new database test also confirms that unlinking a character which is not your active one leaves your active character and hidden address exactly as they were.
items.behind_the_scenes: The routine's last step is now wrapped so that the 'character changed accounts' follow-ups run whether or not the tidy-up succeeds, and the original error is passed on afterwards. The unit test that used to expect the follow-ups to be skipped now expects them to run.
items.risk_notes: This fixes promote review round 1, finding F2. The only effect is on a failure path. A user who hits the failure still sees an error, as on staging.

items.title: One-off repair of hidden sign-in addresses left behind by earlier unlinks
items.where_users_meet_it: Nowhere on screen. It runs once when this release's database migration is applied to staging, and later to production.
items.before: Wherever someone unlinked the character they last signed in with, or an admin removed it, the account's hidden address still names a character the account no longer holds. Each of those characters is one a new owner could have used to land in that account.
items.after: The migration first parks every such account on a private placeholder address that no sign-in can ever match. It then gives each parked account that still has characters the address of its oldest remaining character, unless another account already uses that address, in which case the account keeps the placeholder. No account is deleted and nothing visible changes. An account left on the placeholder repairs itself the next time it signs in.
items.behind_the_scenes: Two database statements. Parking every stale account first frees all the stale addresses at once, so the second statement can't collide even when stale accounts point at each other in a chain or a loop. Accounts whose address is already correct are not touched.
items.risk_notes: This is a pure data repair. A dedicated Postgres test covers correct accounts left alone, chains and cycles of stale accounts, accounts with no links or only malformed links, links on another provider, and a no-op on empty tables. It overwrites the only record of which accounts were exposed. The runtime sign-in repair would catch these accounts anyway; the migration just closes them all at deploy rather than one at a time.
items.owner_question: Before this runs on production, do you want a read-only count or list of the accounts whose hidden address names a character they no longer hold? Those are the accounts that were exposed to the takeover, and the migration erases that evidence.

items.title: The sign-in library's own 'unlink' web address is switched off

items.before: Besides the Settings button, the sign-in library published its own unlink address. A signed-in person could call it by hand to unlink one of their own characters. That skipped all of the site's clean-up: map access revocation, moving the active character, stopping location tracking, and the hidden-address repair.
items.after: That address now answers 'not found'. Settings → Characters → Unlink and the admin tools work exactly as before, because they call the library from the server, which is unaffected.
items.behind_the_scenes: The sign-in library's configuration now lists that one path as disabled. Every unlink therefore goes through the site's own shared unlink routine.
items.risk_notes: The end-to-end test checks that the raw address returns 404 and leaves the character linked, and that the Settings unlink still works afterwards. Only a person's own characters were ever reachable this way.

items.title: Switching your active character checks ownership in the same step as the switch

items.before: The site first checked that the character was yours, then made the switch in a separate step. If an unlink landed between the two, your active character could in principle end up pointing at a character no longer on your account.

If the character turns out not to be yours, you are returned to Settings → Characters with 'That character isn't linked to your account.' That redirect with a notice belongs to the notices change, P255; on staging this case showed a raw error.

The separate pre-check is gone. The character-skills lookup also now uses the existing single-character ownership check instead of reading the whole roster.

items.title: Character ids read from linked accounts are checked strictly everywhere
items.where_users_meet_it: Nowhere visible. It affects how the site reads which characters belong to an account.
items.before: In several places, the stored id of a linked character was turned into a number loosely. An empty value became character zero, ' 12 ' became 12, and a broken id could have produced a hidden sign-in address of 'NaN@eve.invalid'.
items.after: Every place now uses one strict reader that accepts digits only, within the safe number range, and skips anything else. Real EVE character ids always pass, so nothing visible changes.
items.behind_the_scenes: Two small helpers, 'map linked rows' and 'linked character ids', send every conversion from an account link to a character through the one strict reader. They replace loose number conversions and six copy-pasted loops in the account merge, account clean-up, admin user list, background authorization checks, affiliation reads and deletion jobs.

items.title: Corporation-structures reads now show up on the ESI dashboard
items.where_users_meet_it: Only admins see this, on Admin → ESI & rate limits, in the 'Busiest owned-data endpoints' card. Even there it only shows up if something calls the corporation-structures data route directly. No page in the app calls that route today: Settings → Corporations and the industry Custom Structures section build their structure lists on the server instead.
items.before: The card times eight of the nine routes that load a signed-in user's own data: the board, industry slots, industry jobs, corporation industry jobs, skill levels, team skill levels, owned blueprints and owned assets. The ninth route, the one that lists your corporations' structures, answers requests but is never timed, so it never appears on the card.
items.after: The ninth route is now timed as well. If anything requests it, the card shows a bar with its address and average time, next to the others. The eight existing bars keep exactly the same labels, so their history carries straight on. Nothing else changes for anyone, and the route sends back the same data as before.
items.behind_the_scenes: Before, each route passed a hand-typed web address to the timing helper, checked against a hand-kept list of eight. Now each route passes its own contract and the helper reads the address from it, so the label always matches the real route. The corporation-structures route is now wrapped in the same helper. A new automated check looks at every route that reads a user's own data and fails the build if one of them is not timed.
items.risk_notes: Low. The labels for the existing eight routes are exactly the same as before, so the dashboard groups old and new records together. The card shows the eight busiest routes, and nine are now timed. In theory a busy corporation-structures route could push the least-used route off the card, but nothing in the app calls it, so that can't happen today. The route's response is unchanged.

items.title: More precise timing for owned-data reads
items.where_users_meet_it: Nowhere visible. These timings feed the 'Busiest owned-data endpoints' card on the admin ESI page, and that card rounds the average to whole milliseconds.
items.before: Each read of a signed-in user's own data (board, jobs, slots, skills, blueprints, assets) is timed with the server's wall clock in whole milliseconds. The admin card shows the average, rounded.
items.after: The same reads are timed with the server's high-precision steady clock, in fractions of a millisecond, like every other cost figure in the app. The admin card still rounds to whole milliseconds, so the numbers look the same. A server clock adjustment can no longer distort a timing. You won't notice any difference.
items.behind_the_scenes: The owned-data timer had its own copy of the start-clock, record-success, record-failure routine. It now hands each read to the shared cost-measuring helper the rest of the app already uses. That helper gained an optional extra: a small function that adds fields to the success record, which here is the number of items returned. If that function ever breaks, the helper drops those fields and logs it, instead of crashing in the background.
items.risk_notes: Low. Stored durations in the usage log change from whole numbers to decimals. The only reader, the admin card, averages them as decimals and rounds the result, and nothing else reads them. Old whole-number rows and new decimal rows average together without trouble. Two edge cases changed, and today's code can hit neither. A read that failed before it even started used to be recorded and now is not. A broken item counter used to fail the request and now only drops the count. P143's write-up said to keep whole milliseconds; P160 deliberately switched to the shared clock.

items.title: Universe map data files turn away bad version labels up front
items.where_users_meet_it: Not in normal use. These are the three background downloads the map pages use: the solar-system list, the jump connections and the wormhole reference. The app always asks for the current version, which it reads from a small manifest first.
items.before: A request for one of these three files with a malformed version label (one longer than 64 characters) loaded the whole file and then answered 'not found'. If the load itself failed at that moment, for example because the universe data was not yet loaded into the database, the answer was a server error instead.
items.after: A malformed version label gets 'not found' straight away, without loading anything. A well-formed request gets exactly what it got before: the same data, the same year-long browser caching, and the same 'not found' for an out-of-date version. The manifest still tells browsers not to cache it.
items.behind_the_scenes: The three routes were near-identical copies. They now share one small builder that checks the version label, loads the file, compares versions and applies the caching rule. The manifest route sets its 'don't cache' rule once instead of in two places. The wormhole-statics lookup now validates its system id with the rule from its own contract, which is the same rule as before.
items.risk_notes: Low. Responses and headers for valid requests are unchanged. The only difference is for overlong version labels, which now always get 'not found' and never a server error, and skip a pointless load. The map never sends such labels.

items.title: One shared fallback for page sections that are allowed to fail on their own
items.where_users_meet_it: No visible change. It covers the admin dashboard cards, the map page (Atlas) and the job feeds in the industry Profiles section.
items.before: When one of these background reads fails, the page falls back quietly. An admin card says 'Unable to load this section.' The map page shows without the site-search list, or with the map list marked unavailable. The Profiles job feeds show no characters. Each place had its own hand-written copy of this logic.
items.after: The fallbacks and log messages are exactly the same. Redirects and 'not found' pages still pass through untouched, and one failing section still never takes down the rest of the page. The map still tries the full scanner site list first and only uses the lightweight list if that fails.
items.behind_the_scenes: Six hand-written blocks that each read, logged on failure and fell back are now one small shared helper. It runs the read, lets the framework's own redirect and not-found signals through, logs any other failure with the same message as before, and returns the fallback. The map's 'listing unavailable' placeholder is now defined once instead of twice.
items.risk_notes: Very low. Log text is byte-for-byte the same, so any log-based alerting still matches. The reviewer checked every fallback value and the map's three-way sign-in logic (unknown, guest, signed in), and all are unchanged.

items.title: One shared check that drops stale data after you switch account or character
items.where_users_meet_it: No visible change. It protects the data that refreshes in the background: live board and industry data, industry slots, industry profiles and the structures manager. Data fetched for one account or character never shows up after you switch to another.
items.before: If you switch character or account, or sign out, while a background refresh is still running, the late answer is thrown away so it can't show the previous character's data. Each of these places wrote that check by hand, in slightly different ways.
items.after: The protection and behaviour are the same, but the check is now written once. Switching back to an account you used earlier still counts as a fresh session, so a request left over from before is still thrown away.
items.behind_the_scenes: Thirteen hand-written checks in five areas became two named helpers. The first asks: is this still the session that is signed in right now? The second asks: are these the same account and the same character? The structures manager uses the second to compare the page's server-rendered owner with whoever is signed in, and the app uses it to skip republishing an unchanged identity.
items.risk_notes: Very low. The reviewer confirmed that all thirteen replacements give the same results, including when signed out and in the two places that used to skip the signed-out check (they already return earlier in that case).
